When Professors and Students Misjudge a Subject: Reflections on Teaching ENPP

;

Recently, I noticed a professor complaining that he is a master in another subject, yet the college assigned him to teach ENPP — Engineering Professional Practice — a subject outside his expertise. I wonder why the college didn’t give him the subject aligned with his specialization.

ENPP is a new subject for students. Many of them don’t even bother to Google or research its importance. They see it as a low-credit, 2-credit exam subject and quickly label it “bullshit” simply because of that. These students, mostly in their 7th semester, have minimal knowledge about ENPP and even less patience to understand its motive or relevance.

On the other hand, the professor assigned to this subject, as mentioned earlier, is also not very interested in it. This sets a worrying stage.

## Judging Without Understanding: A Student’s Perspective

My question to students is: how can you judge a subject without knowing enough about it? How can the advice of a senior, who might not be interested in the subject, yet secured a top CGPA and a dream placement, be your sole reason to dismiss the course? Maybe you only glance at the surface and miss out on the subject’s depth and real-life applications. What would you lose if this subject wasn’t taught?

ENPP is designed to prepare you for professional practice, a skill vital for your career beyond exams and grades. But that requires effort, curiosity, and an open mind to explore beyond what’s immediately visible.

## The Professor’s Role: More Than Just Expertise

Now, to the professor: perhaps the college didn’t do justice to you by assigning a subject outside your domain. However, what’s more concerning is what happens to the students. By showing disinterest or complaining, you might unknowingly kill the curiosity, enthusiasm, and exploratory spirit of students who come to class genuinely hoping to learn something new.

I understand how frustrating it can be to teach a subject you’re not passionate about. But as a professor, you have the tools and methods to learn from various sources. You can find different ways to access resources, understand the subject deeply, and even teach it in a way that sparks interest — both for yourself and the students who otherwise expect the subject to be useless.

## Professors as Lifelong Learners

When you say, “This is not my domain, I am an expert in another field,” it feels like you’re limiting your own brain’s capacity to learn and grow. You are, in essence, diminishing the meaning of being a professor.

A professor is someone who knows how to teach, no matter the subject. It might take more effort than teaching your usual favorite topics, but you can do it. What it takes is the willingness to put in that effort honestly and do justice to the students who rely on you.

## Learning from Polymaths

Would polymaths like Leonardo da Vinci or Johannes Kepler have complained if asked to study or teach outside their original domains? Certainly not. They embraced the unknown, learned relentlessly, and contributed immensely across disciplines.

As educators and learners, we should embody that spirit of curiosity and openness.

## Conclusion

In the end, both students and professors need to move beyond superficial judgments. Students should try to understand the true value of subjects like ENPP. Professors should rise to the challenge of teaching new subjects with enthusiasm and dedication.

Together, this can transform a “low credit” subject into a meaningful learning experience that prepares students for real-world professional practice.
When Students Shine but Teachers Remain Invisible

;

In every field either art, science, technology, sports, or life skills, learning is rarely a solitary journey. Behind almost every visible skill is an invisible teacher. Yet, it is common to see people proudly display what they have learned while remaining silent about who helped them learn it.

For many educators, this silence can feel discouraging. It can raise quiet questions: Did my effort matter? Was my role insignificant? The truth is far more reassuring and far more complex.

## Why learners often don’t credit their teachers

When people master a skill, they begin to identify with it. The skill becomes part of who they are, not just something they acquired. In this process, the focus shifts from learning to being. A pianist is no longer “someone who learned piano”; they are simply “a pianist.” The teacher fades into the background, not out of disrespect, but out of psychological habit.

There is also a strong cultural narrative that celebrates independence and “self-made” success. Many learners internalize the idea that acknowledging help weakens their image. They may fear that crediting a teacher makes their achievement seem less impressive, less original, or less earned.

In competitive environments, silence can also be strategic. Some learners worry that mentioning an educator gives others access to the same guidance, reducing their perceived advantage.

Importantly, most of this behavior is unconscious. It is not a rejection of the teacher’s value; it is a reflection of how humans frame success.

## What this silence does not mean

When students fail to acknowledge their educators, it does not mean:

- The teaching was ineffective
- The teacher was forgettable
- The teacher’s contribution was small

In fact, the opposite is often true. The most impactful teaching becomes internalized so deeply that learners forget it was ever external. Like language learned in childhood, the source disappears because the knowledge feels innate.

The quiet legacy of good teachers
Great teachers rarely live in applause. Their success is measured not by recognition, but by replication:

- When students think clearly without guidance
- When they solve problems independently
- When they teach others using methods they don’t even realize they inherited

A teacher’s influence often shows up two steps later, in conversations they will never hear and achievements they will never witness.

Re-framing recognition
While public credit is meaningful and deserved, it is not the only measure of impact. Teaching is one of the few professions where success often requires accepting delayed, indirect, or invisible rewards.

That said, learners who do acknowledge their teachers demonstrate something powerful: confidence, humility, and maturity. They understand that excellence is built through connection, not isolation.

## A message to educators

If you are a teacher who feels unseen, remember this:

You are not absent from your students’ success, you are embedded in it.
Your lessons live on in their habits, decisions, and standards.
Even when your name is unspoken, your work continues to speak.

Education is not about being remembered.
It is about making something unforgettable possible in someone else.

I recently enrolled in a course on Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) — an elective that immediately caught my interest. Not because it seemed easy, but because I was genuinely curious. I recently enrolled in a course on Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) — an elective that immediately caught my interest. Not because it seemed easy, but because I was genuinely curious. I saw it as an opportunity to explore a new area, learn something that aligns with my interests, and gain insights into how we interact with technology.

The class is conducted online by a professor who, as far as I know, is currently abroad, possibly engaged in research. Despite the distance, she’s giving us her time and effort to teach this subject. That’s something I respect deeply.

But unfortunately, what I experienced in the classroom left me more frustrated than inspired.

## The Scene

I arrived at the classroom on time, ready to engage with the lecture. But from the moment I walked in, it didn’t feel like a space designed for learning. Students were strolling in at their convenience — 10, 20, even 30 minutes late — chatting, laughing, and treating the class more like a break room than a place of study.

I found my seat, assuming that at least some of us were there to learn. But the noise never really settled. Friends grouped up, phones came out, conversations continued, and students kept entering. No sense of discipline. No sign of courtesy — neither for the professor’s time nor for their own.

I tried to focus. I really did.

## Distractions Win

But the constant interruptions made it nearly impossible to concentrate. The professor’s voice, already coming through a screen, was drowned out by side conversations. I found myself questioning how students in their 7th semester of engineering could be this indifferent to a subject, to the faculty, or even to their own time.

Some might say I could’ve stood up and asked everyone to quiet down. But here’s the thing — many of them are more outspoken, more confident, maybe even more qualified in their own ways. And honestly, I don’t think students at this level should need to be told to behave in a class.

My irritation grew. My friend beside me was scrolling through his phone, just like many others. I felt myself slipping into the same rhythm. But then I paused — this isn’t how I want to spend my time.

I Chose Differently
So, after attending for about 30 minutes and giving my attendance, I left. Quietly. No drama. I just chose to spend my time doing something meaningful instead of sitting in a space that clearly wasn’t meant for learning that day.

And now, I’ve made up my mind — if the same thing happens again, I’ll do the same again. I’ll attend, give attendance, and leave if the environment doesn’t support focused learning.

## Final Thoughts

What bothers me isn’t just the noise. It’s the lack of respect — for the professor who’s teaching us from another country, for the subject itself, and for our own time and growth. We often forget that learning is a choice — and a privilege. And if we treat it like a joke, we only waste what could’ve been a meaningful part of our journey.

To those who care — keep caring. To those who don’t — maybe it’s time to ask why you’re even in that seat.

Until next time.
When to Use DCO (Developer Certificate of Origin) – And When You Don’t Need To
Using DCO is about clarity and accountability. It's a simple practice that becomes powerful when you're part of something bigger—especially in open source communities.

;

In modern software development—especially open source—trust, attribution, and legality matter. One common tool to ensure proper contribution practices is the Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO).

But when exactly should you use DCO, and when is it unnecessary overhead?

Let’s break it down.

## What Is a DCO?

The Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) is a simple legal statement:

> “I certify that I wrote this code or have the right to contribute it under the
>   project's license.”

To comply with the DCO, each commit must include a line like:

```bash
Signed-off-by: Your Name <you@example.com>
```

This line verifies authorship and intent, and it’s added using:

```bash
git commit -s
```

## When You Should Use DCO

1. You’re Contributing to an Open Source Project
   - Many open source maintainers require it (e.g., Linux kernel, CNCF, OpenAPI, Public APIs)

   - GitHub bots can reject pull requests without a proper DCO sign-off

2. Your Project Accepts External Contributions
   - Enforcing DCO ensures all contributions are traceable and legally clear

   - It protects both the contributors and the maintainers

3. Corporate or Collaborative Teams with Compliance Needs
   - When multiple people or organizations are contributing, sign-offs create a paper trail

   - Especially useful in regulated environments

4. Participating in Programs Like GSoC
   - Google Summer of Code and similar programs often require DCO-compliant commits

## When You Don’t Need DCO

1. You're Building a Personal or Private Project
   - If you're the only contributor, there's no legal risk
   - You can track your work without needing formal sign-offs

2. You’re in a Small Team and Trust Is High
   - For tight-knit teams, you might rely on GitHub attribution or internal agreements instead

3. You're Not Planning to Accept External Contributions
   - If your project is "read-only" for the public, you may skip DCO enforcement.

## Common Pitfalls to Avoid

| Pitfall                          | How to Avoid                               |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Wrong author email in Git config | Run git config user.email "your@email.com" |
| Forgot to sign commit            | Use git commit -s                          |
| Manual Signed-off-by mismatch    | Let Git auto-generate it via -s flag       |

## How to Enforce DCO in Your Project

If you decide to use DCO, here’s how to enforce it:

1. Enable the DCO GitHub App
   Link: https://github.com/apps/dco

2. Add contribution instructions
   In CONTRIBUTING.md:

```bash

## DCO Notice

## All contributions must be signed off using:

git commit -s
```

This adds a `Signed-off-by:` line to your commit.

3. Reject unsigned commits in CI (optional)
   Some teams automate this with scripts or GitHub Actions.

## Summary: DCO vs No DCO

| Scenario                       | Use DCO? |
| ------------------------------ | -------- |
| **Open source contribution**   | Yes      |
| **Accepting PRs from others**  | Yes      |
| **Personal/private project**   | No       |
| **Team of trusted devs**       | Optional |
| **GSoC or community projects** | Required |

## Final Thoughts

Using DCO is about clarity and accountability. It's a simple practice that becomes powerful when you're part of something bigger—especially in open source communities.

If you're building alone? Skip it.
If you're building for the world? Sign it.

In a world obsessed with identity, we are constantly nudged to define ourselves. Social media profiles demand bios. Job applications expect summaries of our skills and experiences. Conversations often begin with, “Tell me about yourself.”

Why I Aspire to Be Vegan

Our food choices are more than personal preferences — they shape the world around us. The decision to move from non-vegetarianism to vegetarianism, and eventually to veganism, has been a profound journey for me.

;

Our food choices are more than personal preferences — they shape the world around us. The decision to move from non-vegetarianism to vegetarianism, and eventually to veganism, has been a profound journey for me. It is rooted in empathy, logic, and a desire to live in harmony with the planet and all its beings. Here’s why I made this change:

1. Compassion: A Conscious Choice to Value Life
   My conscience does not permit me to take a life for my own benefit. Watching or knowing that animals suffer and die, often in cruel and terrifying ways, just to become food on my plate, feels fundamentally wrong. Every sentient being, whether human or animal, deserves a chance to live. By choosing vegetarianism or veganism, I honor this belief and embrace compassion over cruelty.

2. Debunking the Protein Myth
   For years, society has taught us that protein comes only from animal products — meat, fish, chicken, eggs, and dairy. This is a misconception. Research has shown that plant-based sources like lentils, beans, tofu, quinoa, nuts, and seeds are not only sufficient but also healthier in the long term.

According to studies, an adult needs around 46–56 grams of protein daily, which can be easily met with a well-planned vegetarian or vegan diet. Moreover, excessive reliance on animal protein has been linked to heart disease, diabetes, and other chronic illnesses.

3. Loving Pets but Eating Animals: A Hypocritical Dissonance
   Many of us consider our pets as family members, showering them with love and care. But why do we not extend the same compassion to cows, chickens, goats, or fish? Is their suffering any less significant? Loving one animal while eating another reflects a societal hypocrisy that needs to be addressed. True compassion knows no species boundaries.

4. The Environmental Toll of Meat Consumption
   Animal agriculture is one of the largest contributors to environmental destruction. Producing meat requires enormous resources, including land, water, and energy. For example, it takes approximately 1,800 gallons of water to produce just one pound of beef. In comparison, growing vegetables and grains is far more resource-efficient.

Moreover, animal farming is responsible for significant greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, and water pollution, making it a leading driver of the climate crisis. A global shift towards plant-based diets is critical to mitigate these effects.

5. The Ethical Concerns Behind Dairy
   Dairy production may seem less harmful than meat, but it is rife with cruelty. Cows are artificially impregnated, and their calves are separated shortly after birth. Male calves, considered unprofitable, are often killed, while female calves are raised to repeat the cycle of exploitation. Milk is meant for the cow’s calf, just as human milk is meant for a baby. By consuming dairy, we are complicit in this system of exploitation.

Plant-based alternatives like almond milk, soy milk, and oat milk provide healthier and cruelty-free options.

6. Evolution and the Myth of Omnivorism
   Some argue that humans are natural omnivores because our ancestors ate meat and we have canine teeth. However, our ancestors relied primarily on plant-based diets, as hunting was risky and labor-intensive. While early humans ate meat for survival, modern humans have the privilege of choice. Our intelligence and ethical awareness allow us to thrive on plant-based diets without resorting to killing animals.

7. The Right to Life: Beyond Humans
   All species, not just humans, have the right to live. Animals are not commodities to be exploited for our benefit. By choosing plant-based diets, we acknowledge and respect the intrinsic value of all living beings.

8. Addressing Common Misconceptions

- “If we don’t eat animals, their population will explode.”
  Animals bred for food are artificially reproduced by humans. In the wild, their reproduction is regulated naturally by environmental factors. Reducing meat consumption will gradually lower their population through decreased demand.
- “Plants feel pain too.”
  Unlike animals, plants lack a nervous system and cannot experience pain. Moreover, many plants regrow after harvesting, unlike animals, whose lives end permanently.

9. Hidden Health Risks in Animal Products
   Animal-based foods are linked to numerous health risks, including heart disease, cancer, and diabetes. Additionally, microplastics and harmful toxins have been found in fish and other animal products, raising concerns about their safety.

10. A Climate Crisis We Can No Longer Ignore
    Our food choices significantly impact the environment. Animal farming is a leading cause of deforestation, water scarcity, and greenhouse gas emissions. It contributes more to climate change than the entire transportation sector combined. Switching to plant-based diets is one of the most effective ways to reduce our carbon footprint and mitigate the climate crisis.

11. The Future Lies in Plant-Based Living
    The availability of plant-based foods and alternatives has never been greater. From lentils and beans to innovative products like vegan protein powders and plant-based milks, there are countless ways to meet nutritional needs without harming animals or the environment.

Let us embrace conscious consumption, driven by compassion and awareness. By choosing veganism, we take a stand for the planet, for animals, and for future generations. Together, we can create a world that values life, sustainability, and kindness.

I stepped away because I realized something profound: I wasn’t getting any real value from it. Instead of offering enjoyment or satisfaction, the game started to bring me nothing but tension, frustration, and a sense of time slipping away.

When I am truly invested in something, I approach it with passion and obsession. But if a hobby or activity fails to give me that spark, it feels like I’m wasting my time. This was my relationship with Valorant. As much as people say it’s a “social” game that helps with socializing, I don’t agree with that sentiment. Sure, friends can play together, chat, and share experiences virtually, but in my view, real socializing happens face-to-face. Whether it’s meeting friends for coffee or having a conversation on a video call, the quality of human connection is far deeper outside of a virtual world.

More importantly, I noticed some disturbing patterns in the gaming culture surrounding Valorant. When people play, especially when they’re in the heat of a match, they can become completely different versions of themselves. I’ve seen people get angry and abusive when they lose, even toward the friends they’re playing with. The aggression is palpable, and suddenly, their relationships, once built on mutual respect, take a backseat to raw frustration.

It’s as if the virtual game world seeps into their real life — poisoning their behavior, thought process, and mindset. And it’s not just the anger when losing; the reactions to winning can be just as disturbing. I’ve seen people gloat and celebrate with excessive trash talk, as if they’ve just conquered a real battlefield. It felt inhuman, watching friends transform into versions of themselves that I never wanted to be around.

On rare occasions, I encountered a few individuals who played Valorant and managed to stay calm, no matter the outcome. But these people were the exception, not the rule. For the majority, a bad match would ruin their mood for hours, even derailing their productivity. I saw friends missing deadlines, postponing tasks, and sinking into negative emotions — all because of a game. That’s when I knew this environment wasn’t for me.

I crave something more productive, something intellectually stimulating. I want to learn, grow, and challenge myself in ways that games like Valorant simply don’t offer. The gameplay felt repetitive: plant or diffuse a spike, fight enemies, shoot them down — it’s predictable. While some might thrive in that loop, I was growing tired of it. Instead, I found solace in playing chess or engaging in physical sports like badminton, football, or even a brisk walk. These activities nourish both the body and mind, offering genuine satisfaction.

Another factor in my decision to quit was a growing desire to switch to Linux. I’ve always been intrigued by open-source software and the control it offers over my computing experience. Sure, there are games available on Linux too, but I knew that once I made the switch, my focus would shift toward learning and personal development, rather than gaming. Valorant, with its addictive qualities, just didn’t fit into that picture anymore.

In the end, I don’t understand how some people make gaming their hobby, especially games like Valorant, which feel so all-consuming. For me, it was a quick decision to quit: I left Windows, switched to Linux, and moved on from the world of video games. Life is too short to get caught in cycles that don’t serve us, and I’m glad I broke free.

Thank you for reading.
Why I Left Social Media: Rediscovering Real Connections in a Distracted World

For many, it’s a tool to stay informed, connect with friends, or even advance their careers. But for me, social media slowly morphed from a helpful resource into a source of distraction, emotional overload, and blurred boundaries. I made the decision to leave — and through that choice, I rediscovered the importance of real-world connections and regained control over my time and focus

In an age where social media seems to dominate every aspect of life, stepping away can feel like an unusual choice. For many, it’s a tool to stay informed, connect with friends, or even advance their careers. But for me, social media slowly morphed from a helpful resource into a source of distraction, emotional overload, and blurred boundaries. I made the decision to leave — and through that choice, I rediscovered the importance of real-world connections and regained control over my time and focus.

## The Allure of Social Media and Its Hidden Costs

Like many, I initially saw social media as a way to gain knowledge and stay connected. I followed creators who inspired me, kept up with college events, and stayed in touch with friends. It seemed like a perfect blend of learning and socializing. But slowly, I found myself caught in the cycle of endless scrolling, saving articles and videos that I never actually went back to. I had fallen into the trap of information overload — acquiring more than I could process.

At the same time, I realized that my feed was increasingly filled with stories and posts from friends that didn’t really resonate with me. I couldn’t understand why so many were sharing random thoughts or trivial moments. These posts, more than anything, began to clutter my mind and take me further away from the meaningful connections I wanted to foster.

## The Problem of the “Unknown”

One of the unexpected downsides of social media is how it affects our perception of others. Before social media, meeting someone in real life left room for curiosity — the unknown remained unknown until you truly got to know them. But on social media, it’s easy to search for someone’s profile and predict their personality, thoughts, or even values based on the carefully curated images and posts they’ve shared. That sense of curiosity and mystery gets lost. I didn’t want to fall into the habit of pre-judging people based on their digital footprint.

I realized that I valued the process of getting to know someone face-to-face, rather than through their social media presence. There’s something special about meeting someone in person, talking with them, and learning who they are through conversation — not through posts or stories. If people wanted to know me, I preferred that they approach me directly, not through a social media profile.

## Learning the Difference Between Friends and Acquaintances

One of the most valuable lessons I learned after leaving social media was the difference between true friends and acquaintances. While on social media, this distinction often gets blurred. We follow each other’s updates, comment on each other’s posts, and share in each other’s moments, but these interactions can be surface-level. When we see so much of someone’s life online, it’s easy to feel a connection that may not be as deep as it seems.

Friendship, I’ve come to realize, takes time to build. It requires face-to-face interactions, shared experiences, and genuine conversation. Acquaintances, on the other hand, are people you know but may not have a deeper bond with. On social media, that line becomes murky because we see both friends and acquaintances sharing their lives, often in a similar way. Leaving social media allowed me to focus on the friendships that truly matter — those that involve real-world interactions and emotional depth.

## Why I Left Social Media

Ultimately, I left social media because it stopped serving its original purpose for me. It became a place of noise, distraction, and superficial connections. I wasn’t meeting people in real life as much as I wanted to. Instead, I was passively consuming updates about their lives without really connecting. Social media profiles became nothing more than notifications or updates — useful only for sharing files or occasional news. Beyond that, it felt like it turned into a constant stream of distractions.

Now, I meet friends in reality, face-to-face. If someone wants to know me, they can approach me and talk. And if I want to know someone, I’ll do the same. There’s a beauty in the curiosity of the unknown, in letting people reveal themselves through genuine conversations and experiences, rather than pre-judging them based on a collection of posts.

## Finding Focus, Clarity, and Real Connections

Since leaving social media, I’ve felt more connected to myself and my goals. Without the constant pull of notifications, updates, or the pressure to keep up with others’ lives, I’ve been able to focus more on my ambitions, aspirations, and personal growth. I no longer feel influenced by the emotions or actions of others online. Instead, I make decisions based on my own thinking and desires.

I’ve also reconnected with the people who matter most in my life. Meeting friends in person, building relationships through genuine interaction, and allowing friendships to grow organically has given me a deeper sense of fulfillment. I’m no longer bogged down by superficial interactions with acquaintances or the endless scroll of irrelevant content.

## Conclusion: The Beauty of Disconnection

Leaving social media has been one of the most liberating decisions I’ve made. It gave me back control over my time, allowed me to focus on what truly matters, and helped me differentiate between real friends and surface-level acquaintances. I’ve rediscovered the joy of curiosity — the unknown that comes with meeting someone in real life and building a connection over time, rather than relying on a digital profile to tell their story.

For anyone feeling overwhelmed by social media, or unsure whether it’s adding value to their life, I encourage you to step back and reassess. You might find, as I did, that stepping away allows you to reconnect with yourself, your goals, and the people who truly matter. After all, life is meant to be lived in the present, not through the lens of someone else’s story.
Why People Use Ubuntu but Still Fail to Learn Linux

Ubuntu is one of the most popular Linux distributions in the world. It’s recommended to beginners, used in universities, and powers everything from laptops to servers. Yet there’s a strange and common phenomenon: many people use Ubuntu for years and still don’t really “know” Linux.

;

Ubuntu is one of the most popular Linux distributions in the world. It’s recommended to beginners, used in universities, and powers everything from laptops to servers. Yet there’s a strange and common phenomenon: many people use Ubuntu for years and still don’t really “know” Linux.

This isn’t a contradiction, and it’s not a failure of intelligence or effort. It’s a mismatch between what Ubuntu is designed to do and what learning Linux actually requires.

## Ubuntu’s core mission: make Linux disappear

Ubuntu’s primary goal is usability. It aims to provide a system where things just work:

- Hardware is detected automatically
- Networking is configured for you
- Software installs are one command or one click away
- Graphical tools exist for most system tasks

From a user-experience perspective, this is a huge success. Ubuntu removes friction and cognitive load. But in doing so, it also hides most of the operating system’s complexity.

## Using Linux vs. understanding Linux

Using Linux is not the same as understanding Linux.

A user can:

- Browse the web
- Write code
- Install applications
- Update the system

…without ever touching:

- /etc configuration files
- Permissions and ownership
- systemd services
- Logs in /var/log
- Process management
- Boot configuration

Ubuntu makes all of this optional. As a result, many users interact with Linux only at the surface level.

## Ubuntu turns Linux into an appliance

For many people, Ubuntu becomes “Windows, but free.”
They install it, customize the desktop, install applications, and move on.

There’s nothing wrong with this but, appliances don’t teach you how they work. When the system behaves well, there’s no incentive to ask deeper questions like:

- Why does this service start automatically?
- Where is this behavior configured?
- What happens when something fails?

Ubuntu’s strength is stability. Its weakness, from a learning perspective, is that it prevents the kinds of failures that force curiosity.

Learning Linux usually starts with pain
Most people who truly understand Linux didn’t learn it from smooth experiences. They learned it by:

- Breaking their system
- Misconfiguring networking
- Failing to boot
- Fighting permissions
- Debugging services that refused to start

Distributions like Arch, Gentoo, or even minimal Debian installations expose users to these problems early. Ubuntu intentionally shields users from them.

## Tutorials encourage memorization, not understanding

Another factor is how Linux is taught. Many Ubuntu tutorials are procedural:

- “Run this command”
- “Install this package”
- “Enable this service”

They rarely explain:

- What a package manager actually does
- How services interact with the system
- Why certain files exist
- How to reason about failures

Users follow instructions successfully but never build a mental model. When something deviates from the tutorial, they’re stuck.

## The illusion: “I use Ubuntu, so I know Linux”

Because Ubuntu is Linux, it’s easy to assume that using it equals learning it. But Linux knowledge isn’t about the distro — it’s about fundamentals:

- Filesystems and hierarchy
- Processes and signals
- Permissions and security
  Networking basics
- Shell fluency
- Debugging and logs

Ubuntu doesn’t require mastery of these concepts to be functional.

Passive use vs. intentional learning
The real difference isn’t the distribution — it’s how it’s used.

A passive Ubuntu user may learn almost nothing.
An intentional Ubuntu user can learn a great deal.

Intentional learning looks like:

- Preferring the terminal over GUI tools
- Reading logs when something breaks
- Editing configuration files manually
- Learning shell scripting
- Asking “why” instead of just “how”

Ubuntu doesn’t prevent this, it just doesn’t force it.

## Conclusion

People fail to learn Linux on Ubuntu not because Ubuntu is bad, but because it is too good at its job.

Ubuntu optimizes for comfort, reliability, and accessibility. Linux learning often requires exposure, friction, and failure. When the system protects users from complexity, users never have to confront it.

Ubuntu is an excellent operating system.
But learning Linux on Ubuntu requires deliberate effort, because the system itself is trying to make learning unnecessary.
Why Readership is Declining Among Gen Z: A Philosophical, Psychological, and Sociological Perspective

As digital technology becomes ubiquitous, there has been a notable decline in traditional readership among Gen Z, born roughly between 1997 and 2012. With access to fast-paced information from platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, books, newspapers, and long-form content are competing with shorter, visually engaging media. This shift has been examined across multiple disciplines, including philosophy, psychology, and sociology, and has significant implications for individual cognitive development, emotional well-being, and societal cohesion.

## Introduction
As digital technology becomes ubiquitous, there has been a notable decline in traditional readership among Gen Z, born roughly between 1997 and 2012. With access to fast-paced information from platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube, books, newspapers, and long-form content are competing with shorter, visually engaging media. This shift has been examined across multiple disciplines, including philosophy, psychology, and sociology, and has significant implications for individual cognitive development, emotional well-being, and societal cohesion.

Understanding the Decline: A Multidisciplinary Approach

1. Philosophical Insights on Changing Values

Philosophically, Gen Z’s shift in readership patterns can be attributed to a cultural transformation in the perception of time, meaning, and purpose. With fast-paced lifestyles, leisure reading often seems like an indulgent luxury. Jean-Paul Sartre, the existentialist philosopher, proposed that people tend to focus on tasks that affirm a purpose or identity. Reading, especially for learning or enjoyment without direct practical application, may seem less purposeful when compared to pursuits that yield immediate outcomes, such as gaining followers on social media or excelling academically.

Moreover, our current digital age echoes themes from Nietzsche, who questioned the rise of “nihilism” — a state where traditional values lose significance. Reading, a historically revered activity, may feel redundant in an era where Gen Z’s sense of worth is derived from engagement metrics and digital personas rather than introspection and knowledge expansion.

2. Psychological Research on Attention and Instant Gratification

Psychologically, the decline in reading can be understood through studies on attention span, instant gratification, and dopamine dependence. Research has shown that human attention spans have significantly shortened since the onset of the digital revolution. According to Microsoft’s 2015 study, attention spans have decreased to eight seconds on average, shorter than that of a goldfish. Reading demands sustained attention and cognitive effort, which may seem challenging for individuals accustomed to scrolling through rapid feeds or engaging with 10-second videos.

Additionally, psychologists have studied how dopamine — a neurotransmitter linked to pleasure and reward — plays a role in the content-consumption patterns of Gen Z. Social media platforms leverage dopamine feedback loops, encouraging users to return repeatedly for short bursts of satisfaction. This instant gratification culture can reduce the appeal of reading, which requires delayed gratification and prolonged focus before the reader experiences the “reward” of comprehension, insight, or emotional resonance.

3. Sociological Shifts in Community and Information Access

From a sociological perspective, the traditional role of reading as a communal activity has eroded. Historically, reading was a shared experience, often discussed within families, schools, or community gatherings. However, in today’s digital age, the sharing of information has become passive and rapid, with information consumed more than engaged with.

Media theorist Marshall McLuhan famously stated, “The medium is the message.” This suggests that digital platforms, with their emphasis on speed and quantity over quality, shape not only how Gen Z consumes content but also what type of content they prioritize. As a result, reading for depth is often overshadowed by rapid content consumption that aligns with social norms and peer validation, creating a feedback loop where reading holds less cultural and social capital among Gen Z.

## The Cognitive and Social Implications of Reduced Readership

The decline in readership has profound effects on both the individual brain and society at large.

1. Cognitive Development and Critical Thinking

Regular reading strengthens critical thinking and comprehension skills by challenging readers to engage in narrative analysis, interpretation, and complex problem-solving. Reading helps form mental models that aid in memory retention, empathy, and decision-making. Without consistent reading, studies show that these skills may deteriorate, leading to a potential cognitive decline and a reduced ability to process information critically.

A 2018 study by neuroscientist Maryanne Wolf reveals that deep reading activates areas of the brain responsible for imagination, empathy, and theory of mind — key for building emotional intelligence and social skills. Gen Z’s shift away from these experiences could result in diminished cognitive empathy and reduced emotional resilience over time.

2. Emotional and Social Well-being

Reading fiction, in particular, has been linked to increased empathy and emotional intelligence. When readers immerse themselves in stories, they engage with perspectives and experiences different from their own, fostering understanding and tolerance. Reduced readership among Gen Z may contribute to what sociologists term “compassion fatigue,” where individuals struggle to empathize with issues outside their immediate experiences.

Moreover, a reliance on digital media for information can foster social isolation, as reading — a traditionally solitary activity that strengthens introspective abilities — is replaced by highly interactive yet superficial digital exchanges.

## Strategies for Revitalizing Readership Among Gen Z

1. Integrating Reading with Digital Platforms

Combining reading with digital technology may be an effective way to rekindle interest in long-form content. For instance, digital reading apps that incorporate gamified learning, social reading features, or even rewards for reading comprehension could appeal to Gen Z’s engagement preferences. Audiobooks and podcasts also offer accessible alternatives to traditional reading, allowing young people to engage with stories while on the go.

2. Promoting Reading Communities and Challenges

Sociologists suggest that belonging to a group or community can enhance engagement in activities perceived as ‘difficult’ or ‘effortful.’ Book clubs, online reading challenges, and group discussions could help rebuild a sense of community around reading, giving Gen Z a shared purpose and social incentives to dive into books and articles.

3. Educating on the Long-term Benefits of Reading

Educating Gen Z on the long-term cognitive and emotional benefits of reading may also inspire them to prioritize it. Psychological and neuroscientific research underscores the positive effects of reading on mental health, empathy, and problem-solving skills. Schools and families can foster these benefits by encouraging reading from a young age, exposing Gen Z to its role in fostering resilience, intelligence, and adaptability.

## The Broader Societal Impact of Increased Readership

If readership rates improve, the positive effects on society could be immense. With increased readership, we could expect a generation better equipped for critical analysis and nuanced thinking, skills crucial in an era of information overload and polarization. Additionally, regular reading encourages empathy, creating a more compassionate society. As Gen Z cultivates these skills, they may become more prepared to tackle complex global issues with a balanced, informed approach.

## Conclusion

The decline in readership among Gen Z is not merely a trend but a symptom of broader cultural, psychological, and sociological shifts in society. While these changes may pose risks to individual cognitive development and societal cohesion, they also offer an opportunity to rethink how we engage younger generations in the pursuit of knowledge and empathy. By making reading accessible, relevant, and communal, society can harness the profound benefits of literature and information for generations to come.
Why Skipping Fundamentals Can Hurt You More Than Help

In today’s fast-paced world of AI, Machine Learning, and Data Science, there’s a growing trend among beginners: jump straight into projects and learn the theory later. It sounds efficient. It feels productive.

In today’s fast-paced world of AI, Machine Learning, and Data Science, there’s a growing trend among beginners: jump straight into projects and learn the theory later. It sounds efficient. It feels productive.

> But is it the right way to learn?

Let’s talk about it.

## The Temptation to Skip the Basics

Many posts and videos today say things like:

> “Don’t worry about the details.” “Avoid perfectionism as a beginner — just
>   start building!

While this advice can be motivating, it often lacks the nuance beginners truly need.

Yes, it’s true that waiting until you “know everything” before starting is a trap. But on the flip side, completely ignoring the foundations leads to a different kind of frustration.

## The Chess Analogy: Why Fundamentals Matter

Jumping into projects without understanding the basics is like playing chess without knowing the rules.

You might make a few random moves. You might even win a game by chance.
But soon, you’ll:

> Hit walls you can’t get past
>
> Make wrong decisions with no way to debug or understand them
>
> Or worse — lose confidence and stop altogether

## Exploration vs. Execution

There’s a difference between exploring a field and building in it.

If you’re just exploring — trying out tutorials, watching guided videos, seeing what excites you — skipping a few details is okay.
But if your goal is to build meaningful, scalable, or production-ready projects, then you need solid fundamentals.

## Real-World Analogy: Software for 1,000 Users

Imagine trying to build a web app for 1,000 users without knowing software engineering principles.

You might get something working.
But chances are, you’ll soon run into:

- Scalability issues
- Unmaintainable code
- Technical debt
- Systems that fall apart the moment you try to extend or improve them

The same holds true for AI & ML.

If you don’t understand:

- The math behind the models
- The assumptions each algorithm makes
- Evaluation metrics
- How training, validation, and testing work…

…then you’re not really “building” — you’re copy-pasting and hoping it works.

## The Balanced Path Forward

Here’s what I’ve learned:

> You don’t need to master every detail before starting.
>
> But you do need to understand what you’re doing at a foundational level.
>
> Guided projects are fine — but take time afterward to dig deeper into what made the project work.

## Wrapping Up The Thought

Strong fundamentals are not about perfectionism.
They’re about clarity, confidence, and creativity.

They don’t slow you down — they save you time in the long run.
Because when things break (and they will), it’s your foundations that help you rebuild stronger.
Why Some People Hate Coding and How to Overcome It

Coding has become a highly valued skill, opening doors to exciting tech careers and empowering people to build amazing things from scratch. But for some, coding is more foe than friend, and the thought of sitting down to write code feels like a chore — or worse. What exactly drives people away from coding? And for those determined to make coding a sustainable part of their lives, how can they move past these hurdles?

Coding has become a highly valued skill, opening doors to exciting tech careers and empowering people to build amazing things from scratch. But for some, coding is more foe than friend, and the thought of sitting down to write code feels like a chore — or worse. What exactly drives people away from coding? And for those determined to make coding a sustainable part of their lives, how can they move past these hurdles?

In this article, we’ll dive into common reasons why people feel frustrated or even resentful toward coding, as well as some practical strategies to help rekindle (or establish) a positive relationship with it.

## The Top Reasons People Dislike Coding

1. The Steep Learning Curve

For beginners, coding often feels like learning a foreign language, where every line must be precise, and errors are unforgiving. The initial steps — learning syntax, understanding logic, and problem-solving basics — can be overwhelming. If the entry feels too steep, people may decide coding just “isn’t for them.”

Tip: Start small and be patient with yourself. Try short projects and set realistic goals. Don’t pressure yourself to master everything at once.

2. Debugging Frustration

Bugs are inevitable in coding. For many, finding and fixing errors can be an immensely frustrating experience. When you’ve spent hours trying to identify a single missing semicolon or stray quotation mark, the joy of coding can start to slip away.

Tip: Consider debugging as part of the learning process. It teaches patience and hones your problem-solving skills. Use resources like online communities or pair programming for support.

3. Lack of Immediate Gratification

Unlike more visible forms of work, the outcomes of coding aren’t always immediately satisfying. Often, it can take hours — or even days — to see a project take shape, and this slow progress can be discouraging for those who like quick wins.

Tip: Break larger projects into smaller tasks. Celebrate each step, even if it feels minor. This can help you recognize progress and keep motivated.

4. Constantly Changing Technologies

Programming languages, frameworks, and tools are constantly evolving. For some, the endless learning cycle can feel exhausting or unmanageable, making it hard to keep up, let alone stay motivated.

Tip: Focus on fundamentals rather than chasing every new trend. Once you understand core programming concepts, adapting to new languages or frameworks becomes easier.

5. Fear of Failure

Coding can feel intimidating. The idea that “I’m just not good at this” can set in quickly, especially if one’s early experiences are riddled with bugs or project roadblocks. This fear can make coding feel more daunting than it needs to be.

Tip: Embrace mistakes as part of the learning journey. Each error is an opportunity to learn. Remember that no one gets everything right the first time; coding is about iteration and improvement.

## Rediscovering the Joy of Coding

If you find coding intimidating, frustrating, or overwhelming, you’re not alone. Many successful programmers started out with similar feelings. The key is to find ways to make coding feel manageable, rewarding, and — most importantly — fun. Explore projects that excite you, seek out supportive communities, and give yourself room to grow at your own pace.

Remember, coding isn’t just a skill; it’s a journey. And every journey has its ups and downs. By shifting your approach and focusing on small victories, you can transform coding from a source of stress to a rewarding experience.

We often say, “This is mine.” My achievements, my failures, my body, my thoughts, my preferences. But if we pause and examine these claims more closely, a disconcerting yet profound truth begins to emerge: none of it is truly ours.

Your achievements are not yours alone. They are the byproducts of your upbringing, your environment, your genetic predispositions, your access to resources, and the circumstances that allowed certain doors to open. Had you been born into a different culture, time, or body, would those same achievements have existed? Unlikely.

Your failures, too, are not solely your own. They are often the consequences of a complex web of conditions — perhaps an absence of support, inherited trauma, or societal constraints. Like success, failure is contextual.

Even your body is not yours in any volitional sense. You did not choose your skin color, your features, your height, or the vessel that carries your consciousness. The body you inhabit was given to you, shaped by biology, ancestry, and random chance.

Your behavior, practices, articulation, and even your taste in music or art are not born in isolation. They are the products of what you’ve been exposed to — the culture you were raised in, the media you consumed, the people you admired, the values that surrounded you. They are conditioned responses, not autonomous creations.

Your choices, the ones you proudly label as “mine,” are often influenced by subconscious programming, by patterns instilled over years of repetition, reaction, and reinforcement. And your thinking — perhaps the most intimate part of yourself — is a collection of borrowed ideas, internalized beliefs, and mental habits shaped by others. Even the perspective that “nothing is yours” may itself be an idea absorbed from philosophy, spirituality, or a conversation long past.

In essence, you are a product of your environment — a complex consolidation of events, inputs, and influences that you neither initiated nor controlled. You are not a sovereign island, but a confluence of rivers — flowing from sources you cannot trace.

This realization is not meant to strip meaning from life but to invite humility. It allows us to understand ourselves not as isolated authors of our identity, but as reflections of the world around us, shaped by countless visible and invisible hands. In this understanding, perhaps, there is room for deeper empathy — both for ourselves and for others.

So, when we say “this is mine”, perhaps it is more accurate to say:

“This is passing through me.”

And if you ask me —

- “Who are you?”
- “What defines you?”
- “What is your identity?”I would answer simply: “I am nothing. Just a reflection of causes, conditions, and time.”
